covers.quote: Use italics and sentence case for titles of plays

examples.note: Play titles in italics and sentence case.

parts.quote: The theme of Williamson’s Emerald city is in stark contrast to that of The club.

examples.note: Play title in italics and sentence case.

parts.quote: Noni Hazlehurst played Kathy in the Sydney Theatre Company’s play No names … no pack drill.

rules.quote: Write titles of plays in italics and use sentence case.
rules.violation_condition: a title of a play written without italics or not in sentence case
rules.why: G-4: body states instruction directly; absorbed candidate heading.

covers.quote: Use a forward slash to show line breaks in plays

examples.note: Quoted lines use spaced forward slashes to indicate original line breaks.

parts.quote: Adita loved to quote Hamlet on days like this. ‘Tis now the very witching time of night / When churchyards yawn and hell itself breathes out / Contagion to this world …’ Her colleagues found these performances tiresome.

rules.quote: When you quote lines spoken by a character in a play, use a forward slash to show line breaks appearing in the original. Insert spaces around the forward slash.
rules.violation_condition: quoted character dialogue from a play where line breaks from the original are run together without a spaced forward slash, or with a forward slash lacking surrounding spaces
when: If there's a line break in your text, it can occur before or after the slash.
rules.why: G-2: absorbed candidate heading and relaxed placement condition.

covers.quote: Don’t use quotation marks in scripts of plays

examples.note: Direct speech follows the character's name without quotation marks.

parts.quote: RICHARDS: You’ve the luck of the devil.
NED: It’s not luck; it’s gumption. We don’t think with our boots as traps do.

rules.quote: In plays, you don’t need quotation marks if the direct speech follows the name of the speaker.
rules.violation_condition: quotation marks used around direct speech in a play script when the dialogue directly follows the speaker's name
when: In play scripts where character speech follows speaker names.
rules.why: G-4: candidate heading absorbed by body instruction.

covers.quote: Use divisions for in-text citations of plays
Citations to plays are more helpful if you use divisions – acts, scenes and lines.

examples.note: Full playwright name with roman, lowercase division names and numerals.

parts.quote: In the words of Breaker Morant, ‘There are things adrift here … alien to justice.’ (Kenneth Ross Breaker Morant, act 1, scene 13)

rules.quote: Use the full name of the playwright, unless people can identify the playwright by the surname. Use roman type (not italics), lower case and numerals for divisions.
rules.violation_condition: an in-text citation of a play that uses an unfamiliar surname alone, italicises divisions, or fails to use lowercase and numerals for divisions
when: divisions (acts, scenes, lines) are available in citations to plays
surname alone may be used if the playwright is widely known/identifiable by surname alone
rules.why: G-1, G-2: combines division formatting and author naming into single coherent citation rule.

covers.quote: Use the edition of the play you cited. If the play was written well before the edition, place the original date in parentheses with the edition’s publishing date.

examples.note: Reference list entry for a play.

parts.quote: Murray-Smith J (2002) Rapture, Currency Press, Sydney.

examples.note: Reference list entry with subtitle.

parts.quote: Ross K (1979) Breaker Morant: a play in two acts, Edward Arnold Pty Ltd, Melbourne.

examples.note: Reference list entry with original publication year and edition year.

parts.quote: Yeats WB (1892/2018) The Countess Cathleen: a play, CreateSpace Independent Publishing Platform, Scotts Valley.

rules.quote: Rule: Author A (Year of Original Publication/Year of Edition) Title of play: subtitle of play, Name of Publisher of Edition, Place of Publication.
rules.violation_condition: a reference list entry for a play that does not follow the format 'Author A (Year of Original Publication/Year of Edition) Title of play: subtitle of play, Name of Publisher of Edition, Place of Publication.'
when: Applies when including a play in a reference list.
If the play was not written well before the edition, only the publication year is cited.
rules.why: G-2: reference format specification covers the conditional original date handling.

examples.note: Author-date citation with page number.

parts.quote: (Murray-Smith 2002:5)

examples.note: Author-date citation for old work with original and modern edition years.

rules.quote: Use the author–date system for in-text citations in documents with a reference list. Include a page number after a colon if you’re citing a specific page. Use the original and edition dates if citing an old work.
rules.violation_condition: an in-text citation for a play in an author-date document that omits the colon before the page number or omits the original/edition date slash format for an old work
when: In documents that have a reference list using the author-date system.
rules.why: Standard citation instruction for in-text citations of plays.

covers.quote: Follow the rules of citation for the source (for example, a newspaper) that published the review. Use italics for the title of the play.

examples.note: Reference list entry for a play review in a newspaper.

parts.quote: Wilkins P (5 April 2019) ‘How to rule the world a timely reminder of issues facing the nation’ [Review of How to rule the world by Nakkiah Lui], The Canberra Times.

examples.note: Online play review entry with accessed date.

parts.quote: Wakelin O (25 January 2019) ‘Review: The big time,Ensemble Theatre’ [Review of The big time by David Williamson], ArtsHub, accessed 18 December 2019.

rules.quote: Rule: Reviewer R (Day Month Year) ‘Title of review: subtitle of review’ [Review of Title of work by Creator], Name of Blog, Newspaper or Magazine, accessed Day Month Year.
rules.violation_condition: a reference list citation for a review of a play that deviates from the required template 'Reviewer R (Day Month Year) ‘Title of review: subtitle of review’ [Review of Title of work by Creator], Name of Blog, Newspaper or Magazine, accessed Day Month Year.'
when: Applies when citing a review of a play in a reference list.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: template covers rules on reviewing play references.

covers.quote: Use quotation marks for titles of poems

examples.note: Poem title enclosed in single quotation marks.

parts.quote: MJ decided his draft was ‘huddled in clichés’ like the writer’s words in Gwen Harwood’s poem ‘Critic’s nightwatch’.

examples.note: Poem title inside a quote enclosed in double quotation marks.

parts.quote: ‘Have you read “Sun orchids” by Douglas Stewart?’ asked Hayley.

rules.quote: Enclose titles of poems in quotation marks. If the title is part of a quotation, enclose it in double quotation marks.
rules.violation_condition: a poem title not enclosed in quotation marks, or a poem title inside a quote not enclosed in double quotation marks
when: Unless the poem is published as a book/freestanding work.
rules.why: G-4: absorbed candidate heading.

covers.quote: Italicise titles of poems published as books
This means you italicise the titles of verse novels as you do for prose novels.

examples.note: Freestanding poem title in italics.

parts.quote: Sky saga: a story of Empire airmen by Thomas White is a tribute to the men of the Empire Air Training Scheme.

examples.note: Verse novel title in italics.

parts.quote: Les Murray wrote Fredy Neptune: a novel in verse in 8-line stanzas.

rules.quote: Poems can be published as a freestanding work in book form. In this case, follow the citation rules for books. Use italics for the poem’s title.
rules.violation_condition: a title of a poem published as a freestanding book (or verse novel) written in quotation marks or roman text instead of italics
when: Applies when a poem is published as a freestanding work in book form, including verse novels.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed heading and explanatory restatement on verse novels.

covers.quote: Capitalise and punctuate the title of a poem as the author does

If you’re unsure of the author’s style, write the titles of poems using sentence case. Sentence case can usually replace title case (maximal capitalisation), which is often a publishing style rather than an artistic choice.

examples.note: Maintains idiosyncratic author capitalisation.

parts.quote: Sue Nicholls’s anthology includes ‘The Moment’, ‘those black sunglasses’ and ‘Joan (ii)’.

examples.note: Maintains original punctuation and capitalisation.

parts.quote: George Ade’s poem ‘R-E-M-O-R-S-E’ begins with the lines, ‘The cocktail is a pleasant drink, / It’s mild and harmless, I don’t think.’

rules.quote: Apply the author’s own style for capitalisation and punctuation. If the title is all lower case or all upper case, follow suit.
rules.violation_condition: normalising or changing the capitalisation or punctuation of a poem's title instead of following the author's own style
when: If unsure of the author's style, write the titles of poems using sentence case.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: heading and fallback condition absorbed.

covers.quote: Italicise titles of filmpoems

examples.note: Videopoem title italicised.

parts.quote: The videopoem Dog Daze is the work of Adelaide poet and former anatomy professor Ian Gibbons.

rules.quote: Italicise titles of filmpoems and use the original capitalisation and punctuation.
rules.violation_condition: a title of a filmpoem (or poetryfilm/videopoem) not set in italics, or altering its original capitalisation and punctuation
rules.why: G-4: absorbed candidate heading.

covers.quote: Use the first lines of untitled, published poems
Use quotation marks as you would for other titles. Capitalise the line as it appears in the poem.

examples.note: First line used as title in quotation marks.

parts.quote: Birmingham included his sonnet ‘I am very bothered when I think’ in the collection titled Paper aeroplane: selected poems 1989–2014.

examples.note: First line of limerick used as title.

parts.quote: Arthur Buller wrote ‘There was a young lady from Bright’, a limerick about relativity.

rules.quote: Even if the poem isn’t well known, use the first line as a title for untitled poems.
rules.violation_condition: referring to an untitled published poem without using its first line as the title enclosed in quotation marks
when: Applies to untitled published poems.
Use quotation marks as you would for other titles. Capitalise the line as it appears in the poem.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed candidate heading and formatting sentence.

covers.quote: Use italics for titles of anthologies and other collections

examples.note: Individual poem in quotation marks, collection title italicised in sentence case.

parts.quote: ‘(Because I am a daughter) of diaspora’ appeared in Eunice Andrada’s collection Flood damages.

rules.quote: If a poem is part of a published collection, italicise the title of the collection and use sentence case. Use quotation marks for the poems in the collection.
rules.violation_condition: a published poetry collection title not italicised or not in sentence case, or individual poems within it not placed in quotation marks
when: Applies when citing a poem that is part of a published collection.
rules.why: G-4: body states instruction; absorbed candidate heading.

covers.quote: Use a forward slash to show line breaks in poems

examples.note: Poem lines separated by spaced forward slash.

parts.quote: Challenged to quote some Slessor, Rita responded in a flash, ‘In Melbourne, your appetite had gone, / Your angers too; ...’

rules.quote: Separate lines of poetry in a sentence with a forward slash. Insert spaces around the forward slash.
rules.violation_condition: run-in lines of poetry cited in a sentence without a spaced forward slash to separate them, or with unspaced slashes
when: If there's a line break in your text, it can occur before or after the slash.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed candidate heading and line break exception.

covers.quote: Use in-text citations for quotations from poems
In government writing, mentioning the poet and the title of the poem is usually enough.

examples.note: Full poet name and poem title in quotation marks.

parts.quote: As David Malouf wrote in ‘As Living Is’, ‘As living is / or Life as we call it / Neither perfect / nor plain …’

examples.note: Parenthetical citation with full poet name and poem title.

parts.quote: The poet wrote ‘… There was enough space, enough / suddenness, as if everything might stay in reach.’ (Martin Harrison ‘Tasmania’)

rules.quote: Always cite quotations in text. Follow the quotation with the poet’s name in roman type and the title of the poem in quotation marks. Use the poet’s full name, unless people can identify the poet by the surname alone.
rules.violation_condition: an in-text citation for a poetry quotation that does not include the poet's name in roman type and the poem title in quotation marks
when: Surname alone may be used if the poet is identifiable by surname alone.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed heading and contextual guidance into the in-text citation rule.

covers.quote: Use divisions if they are available
For subsequent citations, you can use just use the division numbers, without the words ‘part’, ‘verse’ or ‘lines’.

examples.note: Divisions using lowercase and numerals.

parts.quote: Here are 2 of the most famous – and misquoted – lines in poetry. ‘Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink.’ (Coleridge The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, part 2, verse 29, lines 121–2).

examples.note: Subsequent citation using numeric divisions.

parts.quote: (Coleridge The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, 2.29.121–2)

rules.quote: Use lower case and numerals for divisions.
rules.violation_condition: division markers (canto, part, verse, lines) formatted in uppercase or using words instead of numerals in poem citations
when: Applies when citing divisions of poems (cantos, verses, stanzas, lines).
For subsequent citations, you can use just the division numbers without the words 'part', 'verse' or 'lines'.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed heading and shorthand option into the division formatting rule.

covers.quote: Include poems if you’re using a reference list
Use the edition of the poem you cited. If the poem was written well before the edition, place the original date in parentheses with the edition’s publishing date.
As in text, use the original capitalisation of the poem in the reference list entry.

examples.note: Reference list entry for an old poem.

parts.quote: Poe EA (1845/2012) The raven, Arcturus Publishing Limited, London.

examples.note: Reference list entry for a poem in a book.

parts.quote: Taylor A (1982) ‘The cool change’, Selected poems, University of Queensland Press, St Lucia.

rules.quote: Rule: Author A (Year of Original Publication/Year of Edition) ‘Title of poem: subtitle of poem’, Name of collection,Name of Publisher of Edition, Place of Publication.
rules.violation_condition: a reference list entry for a poem that deviates from the specified author-date format
when: Applies when including poems in a reference list.
Use the edition of the poem cited; if written well before the edition, place the original date in parentheses with the edition date.
Use original capitalisation of the poem in the reference list entry.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed reference list heading and formatting conditions into the template rule.

covers.quote: Sonnet X
the first line in quotation marks, as for other untitled poems.

examples.note: Sonnet cited using number ('Sonnet 116').

parts.quote: Shakespeare’s Sonnet 116 contains lines often read during marriage ceremonies ‘… love is not love / Which alters when it alteration finds, / Or bends with the remover to remove.’

examples.note: Sonnet cited by its first line in quotation marks.

parts.quote: Shakespeare’s ‘Let me not to the marriage of two minds’ is a popular reading at wedding ceremonies.

rules.quote:
To cite the sonnets use either:
[8fba5037e663] LI  Sonnet X
[e3cb912d31bc] LI  the first line in quotation marks, as for other untitled poems.
rules.violation_condition: citing a Shakespearean sonnet using an invented title rather than 'Sonnet X' or its first line enclosed in quotation marks
when: Applies when citing Shakespeare's sonnets.
rules.why: G-4: lead-in and list items form one rule specification for sonnet citation.

rules.quote: Use italics for Venus and Adonis and The rape of Lucrece. They are available as freestanding publications.
rules.violation_condition: Venus and Adonis or The rape of Lucrece written without italics
rules.why: Specific style exception rule for freestanding Shakespeare poems.

examples.note: Narrative poem in quotation marks.

parts.quote: ‘A lover’s complaint’ is Shakespeare’s shortest narrative poem.

examples.note: Song from a play cited in quotation marks.

parts.quote: Portia’s musicians sing ‘Tell me where is fancy bred’ (Shakespeare The merchant of Venice, 3.2.63–72).

rules.quote: Use quotation marks for Shakespeare’s other poetic works.
rules.violation_condition: a poetic work of Shakespeare other than the freestanding publications written in italics or without quotation marks
rules.why: General rule for Shakespeare's non-freestanding poetry.

covers.quote: Treat nursery rhymes, fairy tales and fables like books

examples.note: Individually published fairy tale italicised.

parts.quote: Children like the pictures in The Australian fairy tale of the three koala bears and little Goldilocks.

examples.note: Individually published tale italicised.

parts.quote: Maurice Sendak illustrated the Grimms’ tale The juniper tree.

rules.quote: If a nursery rhyme, fairy tale or fable is published individually as a book or dramatic work, use italics for the title.
rules.violation_condition: a nursery rhyme, fairy tale or fable published individually as a book or dramatic work not formatted in italics
rules.why: G-4: absorbed candidate heading.

covers.quote: Use sentence case.

examples.note: Individual fable in quotation marks.

parts.quote: The country cousin is a 1936 Disney animated film based on Æsop’s fable ‘The town mouse and the country mouse’.

examples.note: Individual rhyme in quotation marks, collection title italicised.

parts.quote: ‘Toast for Tommy’ was first published in Thomas Gunn’s Bush nursery rhymes in 1920.

rules.quote: If they are part of a collection, use italics for the collection but quotation marks for individual works. Treat individual works as you would a chapter in a book.
rules.violation_condition: a nursery rhyme, fairy tale or fable from a collection not enclosed in quotation marks, or the collection title not italicised
when: Use sentence case for the titles.
rules.why: G-2: absorbed sentence case condition into collection works formatting.

examples.note: Citation with Anon and title when author and date unknown.

parts.quote: Ashley said she felt like those lizards in a nursery rhyme who’d had their tails removed by ‘a cunning fish’ (Anon. ‘Three lizards went down to a water pool’).

examples.note: Citation with author and title.

parts.quote: Among other lessons, Æsop’s fables teach us that ‘it is easy to despise what you cannot get’ (Æsop ‘The fox and the grapes’).

rules.quote: For direct quotes, include the author and date, if known. If the date isn’t known, use the title. Use ‘Anon’ if the author is unknown.
rules.violation_condition: a direct quote from a nursery rhyme, fairy tale or fable that omits author and date (or title if date unknown, or 'Anon' if author unknown)
rules.why: G-2: covers author, date, and unknown-author fallback conditions.

tags.violation_condition: a title of a poem published as a freestanding book (or verse novel) written in quotation marks or roman text instead of italics

when: Applies when a poem is published as a freestanding work in book form, including verse novels.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed heading and explanatory restatement on verse novels.

anchor.quote: Apply the author’s own style for capitalisation and punctuation. If the title is all lower case or all upper case, follow suit.

covers.quote: Capitalise and punctuate the title of a poem as the author does

If you’re unsure of the author’s style, write the titles of poems using sentence case. Sentence case can usually replace title case (maximal capitalisation), which is often a publishing style rather than an artistic choice.

examples.note: Maintains idiosyncratic author capitalisation.

parts.quote: Sue Nicholls’s anthology includes ‘The Moment’, ‘those black sunglasses’ and ‘Joan (ii)’.

examples.note: Maintains original punctuation and capitalisation.

parts.quote: George Ade’s poem ‘R-E-M-O-R-S-E’ begins with the lines, ‘The cocktail is a pleasant drink, / It’s mild and harmless, I don’t think.’

tags.violation_condition: normalising or changing the capitalisation or punctuation of a poem's title instead of following the author's own style

when: If unsure of the author's style, write the titles of poems using sentence case.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: heading and fallback condition absorbed.

anchor.quote: Italicise titles of filmpoems and use the original capitalisation and punctuation.

covers.quote: Italicise titles of filmpoems

examples.note: Videopoem title italicised.

parts.quote: The videopoem Dog Daze is the work of Adelaide poet and former anatomy professor Ian Gibbons.

tags.violation_condition: a title of a filmpoem (or poetryfilm/videopoem) not set in italics, or altering its original capitalisation and punctuation

rules.why: G-4: absorbed candidate heading.

anchor.prefix: and are usually cited that way.
anchor.quote: Even if the poem isn’t well known, use the first line as a title for untitled poems.
anchor.suffix: The aim is to give readers enou

covers.quote: Use the first lines of untitled, published poems
Use quotation marks as you would for other titles. Capitalise the line as it appears in the poem.

examples.note: First line used as title in quotation marks.

parts.quote: Birmingham included his sonnet ‘I am very bothered when I think’ in the collection titled Paper aeroplane: selected poems 1989–2014.

examples.note: First line of limerick used as title.

parts.quote: Arthur Buller wrote ‘There was a young lady from Bright’, a limerick about relativity.

tags.violation_condition: referring to an untitled published poem without using its first line as the title enclosed in quotation marks

when: Applies to untitled published poems.
Use quotation marks as you would for other titles. Capitalise the line as it appears in the poem.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed candidate heading and formatting sentence.

anchor.quote: If a poem is part of a published collection, italicise the title of the collection and use sentence case. Use quotation marks for the poems in the collection.

covers.quote: Use italics for titles of anthologies and other collections

examples.note: Individual poem in quotation marks, collection title italicised in sentence case.

parts.quote: ‘(Because I am a daughter) of diaspora’ appeared in Eunice Andrada’s collection Flood damages.

tags.violation_condition: a published poetry collection title not italicised or not in sentence case, or individual poems within it not placed in quotation marks

when: Applies when citing a poem that is part of a published collection.
rules.why: G-4: body states instruction; absorbed candidate heading.

anchor.quote: Separate lines of poetry in a sentence with a forward slash. Insert spaces around the forward slash.
anchor.suffix: If there's a line break in your

covers.quote: Use a forward slash to show line breaks in poems

examples.note: Poem lines separated by spaced forward slash.

parts.quote: Challenged to quote some Slessor, Rita responded in a flash, ‘In Melbourne, your appetite had gone, / Your angers too; ...’

tags.violation_condition: run-in lines of poetry cited in a sentence without a spaced forward slash to separate them, or with unspaced slashes

when: If there's a line break in your text, it can occur before or after the slash.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed candidate heading and line break exception.

anchor.quote: Always cite quotations in text. Follow the quotation with the poet’s name in roman type and the title of the poem in quotation marks. Use the poet’s full name, unless people can identify the poet by the surname alone.

covers.quote: Use in-text citations for quotations from poems
In government writing, mentioning the poet and the title of the poem is usually enough.

examples.note: Full poet name and poem title in quotation marks.

parts.quote: As David Malouf wrote in ‘As Living Is’, ‘As living is / or Life as we call it / Neither perfect / nor plain …’

examples.note: Parenthetical citation with full poet name and poem title.

parts.quote: The poet wrote ‘… There was enough space, enough / suddenness, as if everything might stay in reach.’ (Martin Harrison ‘Tasmania’)

tags.violation_condition: an in-text citation for a poetry quotation that does not include the poet's name in roman type and the poem title in quotation marks

when: Surname alone may be used if the poet is identifiable by surname alone.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed heading and contextual guidance into the in-text citation rule.

anchor.quote: Use lower case and numerals for divisions.

covers.quote: Use divisions if they are available
For subsequent citations, you can use just use the division numbers, without the words ‘part’, ‘verse’ or ‘lines’.

examples.note: Divisions using lowercase and numerals.

parts.quote: Here are 2 of the most famous – and misquoted – lines in poetry. ‘Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink.’ (Coleridge The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, part 2, verse 29, lines 121–2).

examples.note: Subsequent citation using numeric divisions.

parts.quote: (Coleridge The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, 2.29.121–2)

tags.violation_condition: division markers (canto, part, verse, lines) formatted in uppercase or using words instead of numerals in poem citations

when: Applies when citing divisions of poems (cantos, verses, stanzas, lines).
For subsequent citations, you can use just the division numbers without the words 'part', 'verse' or 'lines'.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed heading and shorthand option into the division formatting rule.

anchor.quote: Rule: Author A (Year of Original Publication/Year of Edition) ‘Title of poem: subtitle of poem’, Name of collection,Name of Publisher of Edition, Place of Publication.

covers.quote: Include poems if you’re using a reference list
Use the edition of the poem you cited. If the poem was written well before the edition, place the original date in parentheses with the edition’s publishing date.
As in text, use the original capitalisation of the poem in the reference list entry.

examples.note: Reference list entry for an old poem.

parts.quote: Poe EA (1845/2012) The raven, Arcturus Publishing Limited, London.

examples.note: Reference list entry for a poem in a book.

parts.quote: Taylor A (1982) ‘The cool change’, Selected poems, University of Queensland Press, St Lucia.

tags.violation_condition: a reference list entry for a poem that deviates from the specified author-date format

when: Applies when including poems in a reference list.
Use the edition of the poem cited; if written well before the edition, place the original date in parentheses with the edition date.
Use original capitalisation of the poem in the reference list entry.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: absorbed reference list heading and formatting conditions into the template rule.

anchor.quote: Use italics for Venus and Adonis and The rape of Lucrece. They are available as freestanding publications.

tags.violation_condition: Venus and Adonis or The rape of Lucrece written without italics

rules.why: Specific style exception rule for freestanding Shakespeare poems.

anchor.quote: Use quotation marks for Shakespeare’s other poetic works.

examples.note: Narrative poem in quotation marks.

parts.quote: ‘A lover’s complaint’ is Shakespeare’s shortest narrative poem.

examples.note: Song from a play cited in quotation marks.

parts.quote: Portia’s musicians sing ‘Tell me where is fancy bred’ (Shakespeare The merchant of Venice, 3.2.63–72).

tags.violation_condition: a poetic work of Shakespeare other than the freestanding publications written in italics or without quotation marks

rules.why: General rule for Shakespeare's non-freestanding poetry.

anchor.quote: If a nursery rhyme, fairy tale or fable is published individually as a book or dramatic work, use italics for the title.

covers.quote: Treat nursery rhymes, fairy tales and fables like books

examples.note: Individually published fairy tale italicised.

parts.quote: Children like the pictures in The Australian fairy tale of the three koala bears and little Goldilocks.

examples.note: Individually published tale italicised.

parts.quote: Maurice Sendak illustrated the Grimms’ tale The juniper tree.

tags.violation_condition: a nursery rhyme, fairy tale or fable published individually as a book or dramatic work not formatted in italics

rules.why: G-4: absorbed candidate heading.

anchor.quote: If they are part of a collection, use italics for the collection but quotation marks for individual works. Treat individual works as you would a chapter in a book.

covers.quote: Use sentence case.

examples.note: Individual fable in quotation marks.

parts.quote: The country cousin is a 1936 Disney animated film based on Æsop’s fable ‘The town mouse and the country mouse’.

examples.note: Individual rhyme in quotation marks, collection title italicised.

parts.quote: ‘Toast for Tommy’ was first published in Thomas Gunn’s Bush nursery rhymes in 1920.

tags.violation_condition: a nursery rhyme, fairy tale or fable from a collection not enclosed in quotation marks, or the collection title not italicised

when: Use sentence case for the titles.
rules.why: G-2: absorbed sentence case condition into collection works formatting.

anchor.quote: For direct quotes, include the author and date, if known. If the date isn’t known, use the title. Use ‘Anon’ if the author is unknown.

examples.note: Citation with Anon and title when author and date unknown.

parts.quote: Ashley said she felt like those lizards in a nursery rhyme who’d had their tails removed by ‘a cunning fish’ (Anon. ‘Three lizards went down to a water pool’).

examples.note: Citation with author and title.

parts.quote: Among other lessons, Æsop’s fables teach us that ‘it is easy to despise what you cannot get’ (Æsop ‘The fox and the grapes’).

tags.violation_condition: a direct quote from a nursery rhyme, fairy tale or fable that omits author and date (or title if date unknown, or 'Anon' if author unknown)

rules.why: G-2: covers author, date, and unknown-author fallback conditions.
